newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Former Hong Kong policy adviser blasts governor.
newsitem.headline: Former Hong Kong policy adviser blasts governor.

text.p: Political knives were drawn in Hong Kong on Monday when a former British ambassador to China launched a bitter attack on Governor Chris Patten, accusing him of wrecking the colony's transition to Chinese rule in 1997.

In a commentary in the English-language South China Morning Post, Sir Percy Cradock blamed Patten for ruining ties with China and derailing the so-called "through train" -- a metaphor for a problem-free handover.

It came only two days before Patten's final annual policy speech, which is expected to berate China's plan to dismantle Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council and replace it with an appointed provisional body.
Patten's office will respond to Cradock in a letter to the newspaper's editor, spokesman Kerry McGlynn told Reuters.
Cradock said Patten was "deluding himself or wilfully misleading the listeners" by claiming democratic reform was part of China's handover deal with London.
Britain's ties with China soured and handover negotiations deteriorated after Patten became governor in 1992.

Patten expanded democracy in Hong Kong, arguing it was envisaged in the 1984 Joint Declaration treaty between Britain and China on the handover. China disagreed, and it plans to scrap the legislature on July 1, the same day Beijing resumes sovereignty of the colony.

"The facts are that there is no reference to democratisation in the Joint Declaration," Cradock wrote. "There was no bargain or agreement between Britain and China for anything like the Patten reforms."
"He has no claim to stand as a champion of democracy in Hong Kong. He has done it unique harm," said Cradock, British ambassador to China from 1978-84.

Cradock, who also served as Britain's policy adviser on Hong Kong from 1984-92 under former prime minister Margaret Thatcher but left the job soon after John Major became leader, portrayed Patten as an uncompromising leader, a deluded "knight in shining democratic armour" whose criticism of China was as useless as "spitting against the wind".
Patten's office played down Cradock's comments.

"We've got better things to do than get into arguments with Sir Percy, but we're intrigued to see his claim that explicit references in the Joint Declaration to elections do not mean democracy," said McGlynn.

Cradock, his eye on a recent thaw in Sino-British ties and agreements on handover ceremonies -- just 274 days from now -- said London had revived the idea that what matters most is what is best for this capitalist outpost of 6.3 million people.
But "the principal author of the damage" appeared intent to play the "democratic crusader" than to improve Hong Kong's lot, Cradock wrote.
In describing Cradock, the newspaper did not mention he recently joined the board of the South China Morning Post.
Long-time observers of Hong Kong politics said it was the most vitriolic attack they could remember against a governor.
"It resembles the langauge of a Chinese communist political persecution campaign," one said.
"You expect Patten's rival, China's top official here, Zhou Nan, to talk like this, but not a British diplomat," he said.
